title: Why We Write
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Facing the question of whether writing still matters when AI can produce "better" and faster prose, Stuart lays out the mini-sermon case he's building with students for the value of writing in a history classroom that isn't even labeled as a writing course. He starts from a practical rule -- he can't credibly sell the value of writing if students aren't doing much of it -- so he's defaulted his warm-ups to short-answer responses and 10-minute writing sprints. From there he offers four apologetics: writing reveals what a student actually knows and doesn't know; it builds "mental pathways" the way repeated practice builds strength in sports or music; it is the "right work" that produces real strength-building, i.e. practiced thinking; and it lets students explore their inner worlds in a way that outlasts any relationship with a teacher. Throughout, he frames writing's biggest obstacle as simply being hard, which is exactly why the value case has to be made explicitly and often.
points: Stuart's writing-value pitch begins with a practical precondition: he can't mini-sermonize the value of writing unless students are actually doing a lot of it, so his classes now default nearly every warm-up to some form of writing.

His central metaphor is neurological: writing paves "mental pathways" the same way repeated practice does in sports or music, and if he had to pick one lasting effect of his class, it would be an improved network of those mental highways.
He reframes writing as "practicing thinking" -- since all students will be required to think for the rest of their lives, writing is what makes that future thinking more productive and fruitful.

The final apologetic point -- writing lets students explore who they are, since "you'll always be hanging out with you" -- reframes writing assignments like Values Affirmation exercises as motivation-building, not just skill-building.
quotes: But here's the biggest Value obstacle to writing: it's hard. Sometimes unpleasant. Reliably unrelenting in what it demands of the mind.
Writing continues to be one of the most reliable and efficient means to transform the inner world of a human being.
Writing builds mental pathways. I talk to my students a lot about what is happening when we do the work of learning. In our brains, we're creating new pathways through the neuron forest.
When we write, we're practicing thinking. All of us are going to be required to think for the rest of our lives. What we want is for that thinking to be productive, fruitful, life-enhancing.
You'll be done hanging out with me in a semester or two," I tell my students, "but you'll always be hanging out with you.
Writing gets us there, one sentence at a time, just as push-ups build muscle strength and scales build musical fluency.
